source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large pretrained models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions when the format is right (lettered options, few-shot).
numbers: Models 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B. ECE with 10 equal-count bins. The 52B model is very well calibrated on BIG-Bench and MMLU multiple choice, and overconfident only in the tails (true/false version).
limits: Holds for the base model and closed answer sets; not shown for free-form text.
agent_relevance: Stated certainty is only trustworthy when the answer space is closed.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Replacing one option with 'None of the above' hurts accuracy and calibration even for the 52B model, which is biased against choosing it.
numbers: Section 3.1, MMLU and BIG-Bench, 52B, 5-shot.
limits: Shows calibration is fragile to format.
agent_relevance: Test the abstain path separately; do not treat 'no option fits' as a cheap confidence signal.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: A helpful-and-harmless RLHF policy looks badly miscalibrated, but one temperature (T = 2.5) for all evaluations largely repairs it.
numbers: Same T = 2.5 across MMLU, MMLU true/false and TruthfulQA, 52B RLHF policy.
limits: Quick experiment on an early RLHF recipe; later work (Leng 2025) finds RLHF drives verbalized overconfidence.
agent_relevance: Post-training distorts token-probability confidence; recalibrate before using it as a gate.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(True): the model proposes an answer, then rates the probability its own answer is true. Samples with P(True) > 0.5 are far more often correct. Zero-shot P(True) is poorly calibrated; few-shot (20-shot) fixes much of it. Showing the model many of its own samples before judging one improves self-evaluation.
numbers: Sizes 800M-52B; TriviaQA, Lambada, arithmetic, GSM8K, code tasks. Conditional accuracy when P(True) > 0.5 is substantially higher than overall accuracy (Fig. 32).
limits: Easier for larger models; needs examples; checking own answers is weaker than checking a third party's.
agent_relevance: Origin of the 'verify own answer' step. Showing the checker several candidate answers is the part that helps.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(IK) ('I know'): a head trained on graded samples predicts which questions the model can answer, and rises when relevant source text or a hint is in context. It partly transfers across tasks but calibration on new tasks is poor.
numbers: 52B model; in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals.
limits: Needs finetuning on labelled correct/incorrect samples; a scaffold cannot train this.
agent_relevance: A scaffold-only agent must approximate P(IK) with sampling agreement.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 can be finetuned to state verbalized probabilities ('61%', 'medium') that are calibrated, also under distribution shift, and this is not just copying its logits.
numbers: CalibratedMath, 21 arithmetic tasks, trained on Add-subtract. Table 1 (MSE / MAD, lower is better), Multi-answer: verbalized finetune 22.0 / 16.4; zero-shot answer logit 37.4 / 33.7; indirect logit finetune 33.7 / 38.4; constant baseline 34.1 / 31.1. Multiply-divide: verbalized 15.5 / 19.0; answer logit 10.4 / 9.4; indirect logit 11.7 / 7.1; constant 15.3 / 8.5.
limits: Arithmetic only; finetuned model. On Multiply-divide the zero-shot logit baseline beat verbalized on MSE. Zero-shot prompting not tested.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence can be learned; a prompt-only agent cannot assume it.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude), verbalized confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities, often cutting ECE by over 50% relative.
numbers: GPT-4 (Table 2) ECE: TriviaQA label prob 0.078 vs verbalized 1S top-1 0.024; SciQ 0.219 vs 0.201; TruthfulQA 0.445 vs 0.350.
limits: Three datasets; TruthfulQA stays poorly calibrated for every method.
agent_relevance: Ask for confidence in words or numbers; do not read log-probs from a chat model.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: Asking for the top-k guesses with a probability each, then using the top guess's probability ('considering the opposite'), improves calibration on harder sets. Discrimination (AUC) is not always improved.
numbers: GPT-4 ECE (Table 2): SciQ top-1 0.201, top-2 0.140, top-4 0.056. TruthfulQA top-1 0.350, top-2 0.315, top-4 0.198. TriviaQA: top-4 0.041 is no better than top-1 0.024. TruthfulQA AUC: label prob 0.462, verbalized 0.62.
limits: Gain depends on difficulty; two-stage prompting not reliably better than one-stage.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of 'consider the opposite' from the human debiasing work; cheap prompt step.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Vanilla verbalized confidence is overconfident, clustered at 80-100% in multiples of 5, as if copying human talk.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 8 datasets. Average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna. GPT-4 has lower ECE but average AUROC of only 62.7% for failure prediction (chance 50%).
limits: Black-box only; professional-knowledge tasks (law, ethics) stay poor for every method.
agent_relevance: Stated certainty is a style, not a signal. Matches the premise 'consistency, not stated certainty'.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Human-inspired prompts (CoT, step-by-step, top-k) lower ECE, but mostly because accuracy rises, not because the model ranks its own errors better. No strategy wins everywhere.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-4 with CoT: accuracy 93.6%, ECE 0.064 reached by assigning 100% to every item, so confidence cannot separate right from wrong. Mean AUROC for prompt-only methods stays near 0.5.
limits: A constant confidence equal to the base rate scores well on ECE.
agent_relevance: Judge a confidence signal by discrimination (AUROC) as well as ECE.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Sampling several answers and measuring agreement predicts failure much better than the stated confidence. Gains saturate as samples grow.
numbers: GSM8K AUROC from 54.8% (verbalized, near chance) to 92.7% with 5 samples plus consistency aggregation. M = 1 to 13 tested; marginal gain at large M. Pair-Rank gives ECE as low as 0.028; Avg-Conf is best for failure prediction. White-box vs black-box AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522 on average.
limits: Biggest gain on arithmetic; smaller on knowledge tasks. Cost grows linearly with M.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for our design: use agreement across independent runs, not what the model says.

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty
finding: Semantic entropy: sample answers, group those with the same meaning, take entropy over meanings. It predicts correctness better than token-sequence entropy, lexical similarity and the Kadavath P(True) baseline; the advantage grows with model size.
numbers: TriviaQA and CoQA, OPT models up to 30B. Reported as AUROC curves; exact values not extracted in this session.
limits: Needs an equivalence judge (a second NLI model) and multiple samples; open-ended QA only.
agent_relevance: Group answers by meaning before counting votes.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning
finding: Majority vote over sampled reasoning paths improves accuracy, and the share of paths agreeing with the final answer is highly correlated with accuracy, so it works as a confidence.
numbers: Gains over CoT: +3 to +6 points absolute for UL2-20B, +9 to +23 for LaMDA-137B and GPT-3; +12 to +18 for large models on tasks like AQuA. Fig. 5 shows agreement rate against accuracy on GSM8K.
limits: Needs a single comparable final answer.
agent_relevance: Cheapest working calibration in an agent loop: run N, report agreement.

source: Chen and Mueller (2023) Quantifying Uncertainty in Answers from Any Language Model (BSDetector)
finding: Combining sampled-answer consistency with the model's self-reflection certainty beats likelihood, sampling-only and self-reflection-only scores at spotting wrong answers.
numbers: Table 1 AUROC, text-davinci-003, BSDetector: GSM8K 0.867, CSQA 0.743, SVAMP 0.936, TriviaQA 0.828. Self-reflection certainty alone: 0.521 GSM8K, 0.539 CSQA, 0.619 SVAMP, 0.653 TriviaQA.
limits: Company authors (Cleanlab); older GPT models.
agent_relevance: A two-signal gate (agreement plus self-check) beats either alone.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky, Hashimoto (2023) Navigating the Grey Area
finding: Putting certainty words in the prompt ('I'm certain it's', 'I'm 100% sure') lowers GPT-3 accuracy; hedges raise it. Models react strongly to these words.
numbers: 50 templates, four QA datasets, GPT-3 davinci. 21 of 28 templates saying 100% had lower probability-on-gold than the 90% version. Performance peaks at 70-90% stated certainty and falls at 0% and 100%.
limits: GPT-3, injected certainty, not the model's own confidence. Training-text analysis suggests confident words often go with wrong text.
agent_relevance: Do not put 'be 100% sure' wording in the scaffold.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky, Hashimoto (2023) Navigating the Grey Area
finding: Numerical certainty in the prompt is badly calibrated with the accuracy of the generated answer.
numbers: 'I'm 90% sure it's' in TriviaQA gives the correct answer 57% of the time. ECE between 0.30 and 0.50.
limits: Same GPT-3 setting.
agent_relevance: Models treat a stated percent as style, not as a quantity to match.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know
finding: Calibration gap: the LLM's internal confidence is better calibrated than the confidence people infer from its default explanations. People over-trust, mostly by giving high confidence.
numbers: 301 Prolific participants, 40 questions each. Model AUC 0.751 (GPT-3.5) and 0.746 (PaLM2) on multiple choice, 0.781 (GPT-4o) on short answer. Humans reading default explanations: AUC 0.589, 0.602 and 0.592.
limits: Humans see only text, not the number; MMLU and TriviaQA.
agent_relevance: Confident style hides real doubt from readers; expose a separate score.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know
finding: Uncertainty words in explanations strongly move human confidence; longer explanations raise confidence without improving discrimination. Matching explanation style to model confidence narrows the gap.
numbers: Experiments 2a-2c (n = 60, 60, 59): 'not sure' < 'somewhat sure' < 'sure', BF > 100. Long vs short explanation BF = 25. Mean human AUC 0.54 (long) and 0.57 (uncertainty only), BF = 0.23 for no benefit of length. People who changed the answer were 33% accurate vs 39% for the LLM.
limits: Narrowing came from a selection rule on matched trials, partly post hoc; human answer accuracy did not improve.
agent_relevance: Length is a persuasion channel; keep justification short when confidence is low.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone is insufficient. Finetuning on about 1000 graded correct/incorrect examples (LoRA) gives better ECE and AUROC than prompt baselines and generalizes. Zero-shot ECE does not improve as the base model improves; AUROC improves only slightly.
numbers: Open models (LLaMA-2, Mistral). User study N = 181, multiple-choice exam with Mistral 7B Instruct: users follow reliable confidence scores and ignore a random one.
limits: Needs weights and labelled data; user study is preliminary.
agent_relevance: Prompt-only confidence has a ceiling, so lean on consistency and external checks.

source: Leng et al. (2025) Taming Overconfidence in LLMs: Reward Calibration in RLHF
finding: Reward models prefer high-confidence answers regardless of quality, so RLHF teaches verbalized overconfidence. Calibrated reward variants (PPO-M, PPO-C, CDPO) lower ECE at similar accuracy.
numbers: Llama3-8B and Mistral-7B, six datasets. CDPO reduces ECE by over 50% vs DPO; one reported setting shows ECE down 6.44 points and GSM8K accuracy up 2.73 points.
limits: Training method, not usable by a scaffold; two small open models.
agent_relevance: Explains why chat models sound sure; do not trust the first stated confidence.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Reasoning models (long CoT with backtracking) are better calibrated than non-reasoning siblings in 33 of 36 settings, and calibration improves as the chain unfolds.
numbers: 6 reasoning models, 6 datasets. GLM-Z1 has 0.07 lower accuracy than GLM-4 on NonambigQA, yet 0.037 lower ECE and 0.078 higher AUROC. Qwen2.5-Instruct puts over 80% of items in the 85% or 95% bins; R1-Distill-Qwen is near calibrated above 55%.
limits: Verbalized confidence only.
agent_relevance: Calibration gain comes from slow thinking, so an explicit alternatives step is a lever.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Removing slow-thinking behaviours (alternatives, backtracking) from the chain drops calibration. Showing a non-reasoning model slow-thinking examples in context raises its calibration. Qwen3 is better calibrated in Thinking than Non-thinking mode (same checkpoint).
numbers: Ablation on R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, TriviaQA and NonambigQA; single Qwen3 checkpoint comparison.
limits: Causal test limited to few model families.
agent_relevance: Supports a scaffolded alternatives step before stating confidence, no training needed.

source: Tao et al. (2025) Revisiting Uncertainty Estimation and Calibration of Large Language Models
finding: Largest comparison of black-box confidence: three single-pass methods. Linguistic verbal uncertainty ('likely') beats token probability and numeric verbal uncertainty. High accuracy does not mean reliable uncertainty; good calibration does not mean good error ranking.
numbers: 80 models, 0.6B to 671B parameters, MMLU-Pro. Abstract only read.
limits: Abstract level; no per-method numbers extracted.
agent_relevance: Prefer a few ordinal verbal levels over a fake-precise percent.

source: Mielke et al. (2022) Reducing conversational agents' overconfidence through linguistic calibration
finding: Chit-chat dialogue models were poorly calibrated in their expressed doubt, but correctness could be predicted well, and a controllable generator conditioned on that prediction gave a greatly better linguistically calibrated agent.
numbers: Abstract only read; no numbers extracted.
limits: Dialogue models of 2021; needs a trained correctness predictor.
agent_relevance: A separate confidence module steering wording is a scaffold-friendly design.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs matched a crowd of 925 human forecasters on Brier score, while single frontier models had not beaten a 50% baseline earlier. Models showed an acquiescence bias toward yes.
numbers: 31 binary questions. LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60) = 0.19, p = 0.850. Giving the median human forecast improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 accuracy by 17-28%.
limits: 31 questions, one tournament; mean predictions above 50% though outcomes were nearly even.
agent_relevance: Aggregating several runs fixes overconfident single forecasts; watch yes-bias.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval-plus-ensemble system nears the human crowd on Brier score. Most base models are no better than chance (0.25). The system hedges and is weak on extremes.
numbers: Post-cutoff test set: system Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Where crowd probabilities are 0.3-0.7, system 0.199 vs crowd 0.246; worse where the crowd is highly certain because it rarely outputs low probabilities.
limits: Safety-trained hedging limits extremes; retrieval does much of the work.
agent_relevance: An ensemble is a calibration method inside an agent; expect underconfidence at the extremes.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses the model's internal confidence on each reasoning trace to drop low-quality traces during or after generation, replacing plain majority voting. Abstract claims AIME 2025 accuracy up to 99.9% and up to 84.7% fewer tokens.
numbers: Abstract only read; claims not rechecked.
limits: Needs token log-probs (white-box).
agent_relevance: Confidence-gated stopping in a test-time loop; our agent has no logits, so use agreement instead.
